title: Persistent chylous mediastinal drainage when embolisation cannot be completed

purpose: Technical inability to complete an intervention is different from treatment failure. Nutritional cost, leak output, clinical stability and reoperation risk must be weighed together.

prepared_template.title: Persistent chylous mediastinal drainage when embolisation cannot be completed
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her early 40s underwent stand-alone subaortic membrane resection with limited septal myectomy via full median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass. Limited rather than extensive myectomy was chosen because of a relatively thin septal thickness of 1.1 cm. Intraoperatively, excessive mediastinal adipose tissue and suspected thymic hyperplasia were encountered, requiring meticulous dissection with electrocautery and haemostatic clips. Neither pleural cavity was entered. Anterior and posterior mediastinal 24 Fr Blake drains and temporary pacing wires were placed before standard sternal closure. There were no intraoperative complications, and immediate postoperative echocardiography showed the peak LVOT gradient reduced to 14 mm Hg with preserved valvular function.

Relevant comorbidity recorded before surgery: obesity (body mass index 45 kg/m²), chronic tobacco use, vaping, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidaemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus and obstructive sleep apnoea. She had been diagnosed with the subaortic membrane approximately 10 years earlier and managed conservatively while asymptomatic; over the year before surgery she developed exertional dyspnoea and NYHA class III symptoms with increasing LVOT gradients, peak gradients nearly 70 mm Hg on follow-up echocardiography.

On postoperative day 2, after resumption of oral intake, the mediastinal drainage changed from serosanguineous to milky, with output of approximately 400–550 mL over 24 hours. Chylomediastinum was suspected on the basis of the fluid appearance and its timing after oral intake. After this suspected diagnosis, the chest tubes were transitioned from wall suction to water seal for passive drainage with close output monitoring.

Biochemical analysis of the milky drainage confirmed chylomediastinum, with triglyceride levels of 1095 mg/dL (normal <110 mg/dL; diagnostic threshold >110 mg/dL for chylous fluid). Baseline chest radiography and echocardiography showed no pericardial effusion, tamponade or additional drainable mediastinal collections.

Initial conservative management consisted of nil per os status and total parenteral nutrition to reduce chyle production; however, chest tube output remained persistently elevated at approximately 400–500 mL per day.

On postoperative day 8, interventional radiology performed an intranodal lymphangiogram using Lipiodol (ethiodised oil) to evaluate thoracic duct anatomy and identify the site of lymphatic leakage. The study showed contrast extravasation and pooling along the superior mediastinal lymphatic chain, without evidence of a discrete thoracic duct injury. Despite visualisation of mediastinal lymphatics, multiple attempts at thoracic duct cannulation and embolisation were unsuccessful. Given the technical difficulty and the absence of a clearly identifiable embolisation target, further interventional attempts were not pursued.

The lymphangiogram was interpreted as showing pooling of contrast and opacification of the superior mediastinal lymphatic chain on the left side, along the cranial portion of the anterior mediastinal drain.

Alternative causes of milky drainage were reported as considered and judged unlikely: infected or purulent drainage and empyema, given no clinical or radiographic evidence of infection and no pleural entry; lipid-containing drainage unrelated to lymphatic injury, given lymphangiographic extravasation; pseudochylous effusion, given the acute postoperative presentation; and residual haemostatic or topical surgical material, given onset only after resumption of oral intake with persistent milky appearance. Chylomediastinum was the favoured diagnosis because drainage became milky after oral intake, triglyceride was markedly elevated, and intranodal lymphangiography demonstrated mediastinal lymphatic extravasation.

Constructed selected-record review and availability limits: this packet assembles recorded facts from the published case up to the stated decision point (postoperative day 8, after the unsuccessful cannulation attempt). Data were documented at different times and some information is not reported at this point: serial daily drain outputs beyond the approximate 400–500 mL/day figure, trends in nutritional markers, electrolyte or immune status, body weight, fever or white cell count, and the exact technical details of why cannulation failed are not supplied. Unreported data are unknown, not normal, and no pretreatment time point beyond the recorded chronology is implied. No interview or evidence release occurs; this is a static written planning task.
prepared_template.task:
Audience: a clinician. Use 350–500 words in English, including headings. Assess the supplied records at the stated decision point. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
Use these five sections:
1. Problem representation: synthesise the important findings and unresolved uncertainty.
2. Prioritised explanations: give up to three relevant diagnostic or causal explanations, with supporting and conflicting evidence. Do not force three if fewer are defensible.
3. Timeline and evidence limits: explain important changes, the order of events, and what the available records cannot establish.
4. Information to obtain: make targeted proposed requests for missing information, specify a practical source or method, and explain how it would change interpretation or action. Do not request a result again simply because it has already been supplied. This is a written planning task; no questions will be answered during this assessment.
5. Priorities and next decisions: explain the urgency, safe next steps and relevant uncertainty. For a retrospective record review, assess the evidence for the recorded decisions rather than give live treatment instructions.
Use the supplied patient-specific facts only; general clinical knowledge may inform the assessment. Keep observations, hypotheses and proposals distinct. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. Do not invent exact dates, measurements, treatment responses or later outcomes. Do not provide rubric scores.
prepared_template.reference: The patient is described as clinically stable with no pericardial effusion, tamponade or additional drainable collections on baseline imaging; historical leak persistence alone does not establish current acute deterioration. Proposals should weigh the recorded risks of reoperation (infection, bleeding, further lymphatic injury) against the recorded risks of prolonged conservative management (malnutrition, immunosuppression, prolonged hospitalisation), and should not assume the withheld successful regimen.
